data.about: The last task hands over a bare 16 by 12 metre slab with a 100 kN push on it and says: put three walls in, 2.8 metres high, so that it is braced. There is no single right answer, so this view recommends one and works it completely — two walls along opposite edges to take the push and share the twist, one up the right-hand edge to take anything across. With the first force alone that third wall carries exactly nothing, because the two others already line their resultant up with the load. Then a second 100 kN arrives from a different direction and the third wall earns its keep. The panel also offers the layout students reach for first, which is braced and still a worse design: one of its walls ends up carrying 38 % more than the whole applied load.

data.text: form diagrams 1:100 — new structural walls, 2.80 m

steps.caption: EX 10 task 5: a bare slab, a 100 kN push, and an instruction to put three 2.8 metre walls in so that it holds. There is no unique answer — so this recommends one, works it completely, and then shows what happens when a second force arrives from another direction
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: the ceiling plate, 16 by 12 metres at 1:200, and F1 = 100 kN entering at the left edge on y = 3.00 m. Note that height: it is NOT the slab's mid-height, unlike tasks 2 and 3, and the sheet never says so
steps.title: What is given

steps.caption: recommended: two walls along opposite edges to take the push and share the twist between them, and one up the right-hand edge for anything acting across the slab. All three 5.00 by 0.40 metres, all on an edge so they are out of the way
steps.title: Three walls, placed

steps.caption: two of the axes are parallel and the third is not, and no point lies on all three — so the slab can neither slide nor spin: braced. Two crossings, and those two points are where the whole force flow is going to be steered
steps.title: Braced?

steps.caption: the load cannot reach the walls directly, so it is steered into the two crossings. At the entry point it splits into two members, one aimed at each crossing; at each crossing the arriving force is taken apart along the two wall axes that meet there, and each part runs along its axis to its wall
steps.title: The flow

steps.caption: wall C carries NOTHING. Not because it is badly placed, but because walls A and B have already put their resultant on F1's own line — 75.86 at y = 0.20 and 24.14 at y = 11.80 average out to y = 3.00 m, exactly where F1 came in. No eccentricity, no torsion, nothing left for C
steps.title: a) The answer with F1 alone

steps.caption: at 1 cm ≙ 10 kN. With F1 alone every external force is horizontal, so the polygon collapses onto a single line: 10.00 cm out and 7.586 + 2.414 cm back. A force diagram that is a straight line is exactly what "no force across the slab" looks like
steps.title: The force diagram

steps.caption: F2 = 100 kN pushes up through x = 13.00 m. Turn it on in the panel. Now the applied resultant is 100.0 kN at 0°, it is no longer parallel to the two edge walls, and wall C has to close it
steps.title: c) A second force

steps.caption: 2.80 m high, 5.00 m long, at 1:100, with a door — the sheet leaves the design to you. The slab load lands on the top edge and the pin and roller near the base turn it into a horizontal reaction and a vertical couple. Only the pin can take H, so the diagonal always runs to it
steps.title: b) The three elevations

steps.caption: a) A = 75.862 kN, B = 24.138 kN, C = 0.000 kN with this layout. Switch to the task-3 layout in the panel and watch one wall go to 100.0 kN — braced, and a worse design
steps.title: The answer

data.title: EX 10.5 — you place the walls, and one of them does nothing
